name: A Survey of Context Engineering for Large Language Models (arXiv:2507.13334)
publisher: Academic research group, primarily affiliated with the Institute of Computing Technology (ICT), Chinese Academy of Sciences (lead and corresponding authors' email domain is ict.ac.cn); 15 listed authors: Lingrui Mei, Jiayu Yao, Yuyao Ge, Yiwei Wang, Baolong Bi, Yujun Cai, Jiazhi Liu, Mingyu Li, Zhong-Zhi Li, Duzhen Zhang, Chenlin Zhou, Jiayi Mao, Tianze Xia, Jiafeng Guo, Shenghua Liu. Posted to arXiv (preprint, not yet confirmed peer-reviewed/published venue).
date_published: v1 submitted July 17, 2025; v2 revised July 21, 2025 (arXiv:2507.13334). Described by the authors as 'ongoing work,' so later versions may exist beyond v2 at time of writing.
claim_value: Formalizes 'Context Engineering' as, in the authors' words, 'a formal discipline that transcends simple prompt design to encompass the systematic optimization of information payloads for LLMs.' Builds a taxonomy with two main axes: foundational components (context retrieval and generation, context processing, context management) and system implementations (RAG, memory systems, tool-integrated reasoning, multi-agent systems). The paper is 166 pages and its reference list runs to roughly 1,400 cited papers, reviewed and synthesized into the taxonomy. A headline finding is a stated capability imbalance: current models show strong context comprehension but comparatively weaker ability to generate long, sophisticated, context-grounded output, which the authors flag as a priority gap for future work.
claim_definition: This is a taxonomy/survey-opinion claim, not a benchmark result: the authors are proposing a classification scheme for the field and synthesizing existing literature under it, not reporting a new experiment. The '1,400 citations' figure in the task description refers to the number of papers this survey cites and analyzes (its own reference list), not the number of times other papers have since cited this survey; conflating the two is a likely source of confusion in casual citation.
reproducibility: Not an empirical/benchmark claim in the reproducibility sense; the paper is a literature synthesis. The authors do maintain a public companion resource (the 'Awesome-Context-Engineering' GitHub repository referenced in the paper) that lists the papers covered, which makes the survey's coverage checkable/auditable by others, but there is no experiment here to independently replicate.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: No. The authors are academic researchers at ICT/Chinese Academy of Sciences (and other academic affiliations); the paper discloses no commercial sponsor, and the authors do not appear to sell a context-engineering, vector-database, or memory/caching product. [uncertain: a full funding/acknowledgments disclosure was not visible in the fetched content, so a minor grant or lab sponsorship cannot be fully ruled out.]
conflict_notes: The task description states '14 authors'; the actual byline lists 15 authors (Lingrui Mei through Shenghua Liu). This is a minor but checkable discrepancy worth correcting if cited. Separately, the widely-repeated 'roughly 1,400 citations' figure should be stated precisely as the survey's own reference count (papers it cites), not citations received by the survey; several secondary mentions blur this distinction, which risks overstating the survey's influence/reception if taken as citation count in the normal (cited-by) sense.
relationship: Complicates the 'prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now' framing rather than simply supporting it: the survey treats context engineering as a genuine, broader engineering discipline (retrieval, generation, processing, management) rather than a rebrand of prompting, which supports the stronger framing in spirit, but its own headline finding (strong comprehension, weak long-form generation) is a limitations finding about current LLMs, not a triumphant claim that context engineering has solved output quality. It is useful as an academic counterweight to vendor-blog claims precisely because it treats the term as real taxonomy work rather than marketing language, while still surfacing where the field falls short.
derivative_of: Explicitly builds on and systematizes prior work in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), memory-augmented LLM systems, tool-use/tool-integrated reasoning, and multi-agent LLM systems; it is a synthesis/taxonomy of roughly 1,400 prior papers across these lines rather than a single extension of one prior benchmark or framework. It post-dates (by about three to four weeks) the Lütke/Karpathy X exchange of June 2025 that popularized the term 'context engineering,' and the survey can reasonably be read as the academic field's attempt to formalize a term that originated informally on social media.
register: academic researcher (written as a formal literature survey with a taxonomy, aimed at researchers and, secondarily, engineers building production LLM systems who want a structured map of the field)
notes: Verified directly against the arXiv abstract page and PDF rather than relying on secondary paraphrase: confirmed submission/revision dates (July 17 and July 21, 2025), full 15-person author list, 166-page length, and the taxonomy's four-part structure (retrieval, generation, processing, management) plus the two system-implementation categories (RAG, multi-agent systems) mentioned in the task description. The author-count discrepancy (14 claimed vs. 15 actual) and the 'citations' ambiguity (reference-list size vs. cited-by count) are both flagged above as corrections to carry into any citing essay.
new_angle: Corrects the author count (15, not 14) and clarifies that the 'roughly 1,400 citations' figure is the survey's own reference list, not a citation count the survey has received, which is a distinction worth making explicit given this research set's general caution about vague or inflated secondary-source statistics. Also surfaces the paper's own headline limitation finding (models comprehend context well but generate long sophisticated output comparatively poorly), which is a useful, specific counterweight to assert against breezier vendor claims that context engineering has already solved output quality.
